steps.title: Image = desired state
steps.body: A cluster image combines: **ESXi base image** (version), **vendor add-on** (OEM drivers/tools), optional **firmware and drivers add-on** (via a vendor Hardware Support Manager) and extra **components**. vLCM checks compliance and remediates hosts to match.

steps.title: Baselines
steps.body: Baseline-based management (patch/upgrade baselines) still exists in vSphere 8 but is **deprecated**; plan to move clusters to images. Switching a cluster to images is one-way.

steps.title: Remediation flow
steps.body: Compliance check → **pre-check** (HA/DRS, maintenance mode feasibility, hardware compatibility) → optional **staging** (pre-copy payload) → **remediate** host by host: enter maintenance mode (DRS evacuates), apply, reboot (or **Quick Boot** on supported hardware), exit maintenance mode.

courses.title: vSphere certificates without fear
courses.summary: VMCA modes, machine SSL and solution certificates, ESXi host certificates, checking expiry from the appliance, renewals, and the 'everything broke at midnight' certificate expiry ticket.
outcomes: Learners can describe VMCA modes and certificate types
Learners can check certificate expiry with vecs-cli
Learners can plan host and vCenter certificate renewal
Learners can resolve an expired-certificate incident

scenes.text: New admins see 'Your connection is not private' on vCenter.
Because the VMCA root isn't trusted on their PCs.

steps.title: Pieces
steps.body:
- **VMCA**: vCenter's built-in CA; issues host and solution certificates.
- **VECS**: VMware Endpoint Certificate Store on the appliance (stores like MACHINE_SSL_CERT, TRUSTED_ROOTS, solution users).
- **Machine SSL certificate**: the certificate users see on https://vcenter (reverse proxy).
- **Solution user certificates**: internal service identities.
- **STS signing certificate**: used by SSO to sign tokens; if it expires, logins fail.

steps.title: Modes
steps.body:
- VMCA as root (default).
- VMCA as **subordinate** of your enterprise CA.
- **Custom** (third-party) certificates.
- **Hybrid** (common): enterprise-CA-signed machine SSL for users, VMCA for hosts/solutions. Then distribute trust: download the VMCA root (https://vcenter/certs/download.zip) and deploy via GPO.

courses.title: Hardening ESXi & vCenter
courses.summary: Reduce attack surface: lockdown modes and exception users, SSH/Shell policy, timeouts and account lockout, Secure Boot/TPM, least privilege, ransomware-aware design, and a brute-force ticket.
outcomes: Learners can configure lockdown mode correctly
Learners can set ESXi advanced security settings
Learners can audit hosts with PowerCLI
Learners can respond to suspicious ESXi login activity

scenes.text: Attack groups increasingly target ESXi to encrypt many VMs at once.
Contoso reviews its hardening against the vSphere Security Configuration Guide.

steps.title: Key controls
steps.body:
- **Lockdown mode**: Normal (only vCenter + DCUI; exception users allowed) or Strict (DCUI also disabled).
- **SSH and ESXi Shell** disabled by default; enable only temporarily; set timeouts.
- **Account lockout** after failed logins; strong root password stored in a vault; separate per-host passwords.
- **Secure Boot** + **TPM 2.0** for boot integrity and protecting configuration.
- Management network isolated (no user access; jump hosts only); firewall allowed-IP lists.
- Patch promptly (VMSA advisories), least-privilege roles, MFA via identity federation for vCenter.

steps.title: Don't lock yourself out
steps.body: In **Strict** lockdown with vCenter down and no exception users, the only way back may be a reinstall. Plan exception users and break-glass procedures.

steps.title: States

courses.title: Datastore full: paused VMs & recovery
courses.summary: When a datastore hits 100%: why thin/snapshotted VMs pause, how to free space safely, answer the VM question to resume, and prevent recurrence.
outcomes: Learners can explain why VMs pause on a full datastore

scenes.text: At 10:02 several VMs froze with a yellow question icon.
Message: 'There is no more space for virtual disk … Retry / Cancel'.

steps.title: Mechanics
steps.body: A VM whose **thin disk** or **snapshot delta** needs a new block on a full datastore can't write; ESXi **pauses** it and raises a question. Thick-provisioned VMs without snapshots keep running (blocks preallocated). Powering on any VM also needs space for its **.vswp**.

steps.title: Safe ways to free space
steps.body:
- Storage vMotion a non-critical VM to another datastore (if that VM isn't paused).
- Delete stale ISOs, old logs, orphaned VMDKs (verify!).
- Expand the LUN/datastore.
- Deleting a large snapshot needs I/O and sometimes temporary space — not the first move on a 100% datastore.

steps.title: Never
steps.body: Never delete `-flat.vmdk`, `.vswp` of running VMs, or delta files manually — that destroys data.

statements.s: Thick eager-zeroed VMs without snapshots keep running when the datastore fills.
Manually deleting -000001.vmdk files is a safe way to free space.
After freeing space you must answer the VM question with Retry.
Powering on a VM never needs datastore space.

quiz.q: VMs most likely to pause on a full datastore?
options: Thin disks or VMs with snapshots

quiz.q: Best first move to free space quickly?
options: Storage vMotion a healthy non-critical VM off, or expand the datastore

quiz.q: Answer to resume a paused VM?
Why not start with deleting a huge snapshot?
options: Consolidation is I/O heavy and may need space; risky at 100%

courses.summary: All Paths Down vs Permanent Device Loss: how ESXi detects them, timeouts, VMCP responses, the correct LUN decommission procedure that prevents them, and an APD incident.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish APD from PDL by symptoms and sense codes

scenes.text: Storage removed a LUN without telling the vSphere team. Hosts started logging APD.

steps.title: APD — All Paths Down
steps.body: All paths to a device are down and the array gives **no** indication whether it's permanent. ESXi assumes it may come back: I/O is retried. After the **APD timeout (140 s default, Misc.APDTimeout)**, non-VM I/O (e.g. hostd operations) is fast-failed so the host stays manageable; VM I/O keeps retrying (guests may hang).

steps.title: PDL — Permanent Device Loss
steps.body: The array responds with SCSI sense codes saying the device is gone, typically **0x5 0x25 0x0 (LOGICAL UNIT NOT SUPPORTED)**. ESXi marks the device permanently lost; I/O fails immediately.

steps.title: VMCP (HA VM Component Protection)
steps.body: HA can respond: **PDL** → power off and restart VMs on hosts that still see the storage. **APD** → after the APD timeout plus a configurable delay, issue events / power off and restart (conservative or aggressive).

steps.title: Cause #1
steps.body: Unpresenting a LUN on the array before unmounting the datastore and detaching the device on every host.

steps.title: Key choices
steps.body:

- **NIC**: **VMXNET3** (paravirtual) for performance; E1000E only for OS install without drivers.
- **Disk controller**: **PVSCSI** for I/O-heavy VMs; NVMe controller also available. Up to 4 SCSI controllers — spread busy disks.
- **vCPU**: start small; match vNUMA (do not exceed a physical NUMA node unless needed).

story.title: 'I took a snapshot, so it's backed up'

scenes.text: A developer took a snapshot 'as backup' four months ago.
The delta file is now 900 GB and the datastore is at 94%.

steps.title: Mechanics
steps.body: Taking a snapshot freezes the base disk; new writes go to a **delta disk** (`vmname-000001.vmdk`, SEsparse on VMFS-6). Metadata in `.vmsd`; optional memory state in `.vmsn` (plus a `.vmem` style file). Each new snapshot adds a link to the chain.

steps.title: Not a backup
steps.body: Deltas depend on the base disk on the same datastore. If the datastore or base disk is lost, the snapshot is useless. Backups go to separate storage with retention.

steps.title: Best practice
steps.body:
- Keep for as short as possible (common guideline: **≤ 72 hours**).
- Avoid long chains (maximum supported 32; keep to 2–3).
- Large/old deltas slow I/O and make deletion (consolidation) long and I/O-heavy.
- Quiesced snapshots (via Tools/VSS) give application-consistent states for backup tools.

statements.s: A snapshot is a full copy of the VM's disks.
statements.why: It's a delta from the point in time.

statements.s: Deleting a snapshot merges its changes into the parent disk.
Snapshots protect you if the datastore fails.
Keeping a snapshot for months can degrade VM performance.
Reverting to a snapshot discards changes made after it.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:

lessons.title: Forest, domains, OUs, sites and FSMO

scenes.text: Your architect draws: one forest, one domain contoso.local, three sites (HQ, Pune, Chennai), OUs per department.
'Why OUs and not groups? Why sites?' — today you learn why.

steps.title: Logical structure
steps.body:
- **Forest**: security boundary; shares one schema and global catalog.
- **Domain**: replication and administrative partition; contoso.local.
- **OU**: container for delegation of admin rights and linking Group Policy.
- **Groups**: grant permissions. OUs do NOT grant access to resources.

steps.title: Physical structure
steps.body: **Sites** map IP subnets to locations so clients use a nearby DC and replication across slow links is scheduled. Intra-site replication is near-real-time (change notification); inter-site follows site link schedules.

steps.title: FSMO roles
steps.body: Forest-wide: **Schema master**, **Domain naming master**. Domain-wide: **PDC emulator** (time root, password changes urgency, lockout processing), **RID master** (hands out RID pools for new SIDs), **Infrastructure master** (cross-domain references).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Designing OUs to mirror the org chart exactly (instead of admin delegation and GPO needs); one DC only — no redundancy.

steps.body: Many users, one site, time-related errors → time hierarchy for that site. Check the site DC's source and offset vs the PDC.

steps.title: Typical cause
steps.body: A virtualised branch DC syncing time from its host whose clock drifted, or a firewall blocking UDP 123 to the PDC.

- Ask **what changed** (changes, patches, moves) — most incidents follow a change.
- Gather evidence at each layer before acting and keep a timestamped work log.
- Escalate early with facts when the fix needs rights or a change you don't own.

lessons.title: Lab: Group scopes and types

scenes.text: A new junior creates every group as 'Global Security' and nests them randomly. Access reviews are a nightmare.
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: Scopes
steps.body:
- **Global**: members from its own domain; can be used anywhere in the forest. Use for **roles** (GG-Finance-Staff).
- **Domain local**: members from anywhere in the forest/trusts; usable only in its own domain. Use for **resource permissions** (DL-FS01-Finance-RW).
- **Universal**: members from any domain in the forest; stored in the global catalog. Use to aggregate across domains.

lessons.title: Lab: Password and lockout policy maths

scenes.text: Users complain: 'I typed wrong twice and got locked!' Policy says threshold 5. Something else is also trying.

steps.title: Settings
steps.body:
- **Account lockout threshold**: bad attempts allowed before lockout (0 = never lock).
- **Reset account lockout counter after**: the observation window for counting bad attempts.
- **Account lockout duration**: how long it stays locked (0 = until an admin unlocks).
The domain-wide password and lockout policy comes from a GPO linked at the domain (by default the Default Domain Policy).

steps.title: Fine-grained password policies
steps.body: PSOs (`New-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy`) apply to users or global security groups; when several apply, the **lowest precedence number wins**. Check with `Get-ADUserResultantPasswordPolicy user`.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Threshold 5, window 15 min. BadLogonCount is already 3 (an old phone kept trying). The user can afford only 5 − 3 = **2** more wrong attempts before lockout — which explains 'locked after two typos'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Linking a password policy GPO to an OU and expecting it to change domain users' password rules (only domain-linked / PSOs do); confusing BadLogonCount (per DC, not replicated) with total attempts.

lessons.title: Lab: Processing order: LSDOU, inheritance, enforcement

scenes.text: Domain GPO sets the screen lock to 15 min; the Finance OU GPO sets 5 min. Which wins on a Finance PC?
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: LSDOU
steps.body: Policies apply in order **Local → Site → Domain → OU (parent to child)**. Later ones overwrite earlier ones for the same setting, so the closest OU usually wins. Within one container, link order 1 has the highest precedence (applied last).

steps.title: Inheritance controls
steps.body: **Block Inheritance** on an OU stops parent GPOs from applying — except those marked **Enforced**, which cannot be blocked and win over child settings.

steps.title: Timing
steps.body: Computer settings apply at startup, user settings at logon, then background refresh every 90 minutes with a random 0–30 minute offset (domain controllers: every 5 minutes). Some settings (software install, folder redirection, drive-letter changes) need a restart or logon.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Putting user settings in a GPO linked to an OU that contains only computers (they won't apply, unless loopback); overusing Enforced.

To target a group: add the group with Apply (`Set-GPPermission -Name X -TargetName GG-Finance-Laptops -TargetType Group -PermissionLevel GpoApply`) and remove Apply from Authenticated Users — but **keep Read for Authenticated Users or Domain Computers**: since the MS16-072 update, user policies are read in the computer's security context.

steps.title: WMI filters

lessons.title: How Windows is put together

story.title: Arjun's first day on the desk

scenes.text: Arjun joins a service desk. His lead says: 'Every ticket is about one of five things — the user, the app, the OS, the network or the hardware.'
To work fast he first needs a mental map of Windows itself.

steps.title: The layers
steps.body:
- **Hardware + firmware (UEFI)** starts the PC and hands over to the boot manager.
- **Kernel and drivers** (kernel mode) control memory, CPU and devices. A bad driver here can crash the whole machine (blue screen).
- **Services** are background programs (Print Spooler, DHCP Client, Windows Update) started by the Service Control Manager.
- **User mode apps** (Explorer, Outlook, Teams) run per user and cannot crash the kernel directly.

steps.title: Where settings live
steps.body: The **registry** is a hierarchical database: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (machine-wide) and HKEY_CURRENT_USER (the signed-in user). Group Policy, apps and Windows itself write here. **Profiles** live in C:\Users\<name> and hold the user's desktop, documents, AppData and NTUSER.DAT (their HKCU hive).

steps.title: Editions matter
steps.body: Home cannot join an Active Directory domain or use Group Policy; Pro, Enterprise and Education can. BitLocker management, AppLocker and many enterprise features need Pro/Enterprise. Always check the edition (winver or systeminfo) before promising a fix.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Editing the registry without exporting the key first.
- Assuming a user's problem is 'the network' before checking whether other users are affected.
- Rebooting a shared server to 'see if it helps' — on clients it is often fine, on servers it needs a change.

cards.back: Where the kernel and drivers run; a fault here causes a stop error (BSOD)
Background program managed by the Service Control Manager (services.msc)
Registry hive for the signed-in user, loaded from NTUSER.DAT
C:\Users\<name> — the user's files and settings
Shows the Windows version and build quickly

steps.title: Verb-Noun and discovery

steps.title: The four types
steps.body:
- **Local account** — exists only in that PC's SAM database.
- **Domain account** — lives in Active Directory; authenticated by a domain controller (Kerberos).
- **Microsoft Entra ID (work) account** — cloud identity; device can be Entra-joined or hybrid-joined.

steps.title: SID

steps.title: How to check
steps.body: `whoami /user` shows the SID; `dsregcmd /status` shows AzureAdJoined / DomainJoined state.

steps.title: Common mistakes

lessons.title: Lab: Temporary profile after sign-in

scenes.text: Pooja signs in and her desktop is empty with a note: 'You've been signed in with a temporary profile.'
Her files are not gone — Windows just could not load her profile.

steps.title: What happened
steps.body: When the User Profile Service cannot load a profile (corrupt NTUSER.DAT, file locked by antivirus, bad registry entry) it logs Event ID 1511 and loads a temporary profile from C:\Users\TEMP. Anything saved there is lost at sign-out.

steps.title: The registry fix
steps.body: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ProfileList has one key per SID. A duplicate key ending in **.bak** is a classic cause: the real profile is in the .bak key. Back up, remove the empty duplicate, rename .bak, check ProfileImagePath and State=0, then reboot.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Telling the user to keep working (temp profile data is discarded).
- Deleting C:\Users\pooja.r — that is the real data.
- Editing ProfileList without exporting it first.

ticket.short: Desktop empty, files missing after login
ticket.description: Hi, today when I logged in all my desktop icons and files are gone and there is a message about temporary profile?? I have the appraisal letters on desktop, please urgent!!

investigate.label: Check Event Viewer > Application for User Profile Service events
investigate.reveal: Event 1511: Windows cannot find the local profile and is logging you on with a temporary profile.

investigate.label: Look in C:\Users
investigate.reveal: C:\Users\pooja.r exists, 6.2 GB, Desktop folder has 48 files. C:\Users\TEMP also exists.

investigate.label: Check ProfileList in the registry
investigate.reveal: Two keys: S-1-5-21-…-4412 (ProfileImagePath C:\Users\TEMP) and S-1-5-21-…-4412.bak (ProfileImagePath C:\Users\pooja.r).

investigate.label: Ask if her Wi-Fi is working
investigate.reveal: Yes, she can browse the web normally.

investigate.label: Reset her AD password
investigate.reveal: Not related — she signed in successfully.

options: Her AD account is locked out
The files were deleted by ransomware
Her real profile's ProfileList entry was renamed to .bak and a temporary entry took its place
diagnosis.why: Event 1511 + duplicate SID key with .bak is the classic temp-profile pattern.

resolution: Tell the user not to save anything in the temporary session and sign her out
Sign in as an admin and export the ProfileList key as a backup
Delete the duplicate SID key that points to C:\Users\TEMP
Rename the .bak key by removing .bak and confirm ProfileImagePath is C:\Users\pooja.r
Set RefCount and State to 0 in that key
Restart, have the user sign in and confirm desktop files are back

closure.prompt: Write the resolution / closure note for this ticket
closure.model: Root cause: duplicate ProfileList entry (.bak) made Windows load a temporary profile (Event 1511). Fix: exported ProfileList, removed the TEMP duplicate key, renamed the .bak key, reset State/RefCount to 0. Verification: user signed in, 48 desktop files present, no new 1511 events. Advised user to also store work files in OneDrive.

lessons.title: How Windows printing works

story.title: Where does a print job go?

scenes.text: Meera clicks Print. Seconds later the page appears on a printer two floors away.
Between those two moments: app → spooler → driver → port → print server → device.

steps.title: The path
steps.body:
- The app renders via the **printer driver** (v3 or v4 / class driver).
- The **Print Spooler** service (spoolsv.exe) queues jobs in C:\Windows\System32\spool\PRINTERS (.SPL/.SHD files).
- A **port** (Standard TCP/IP port 9100 RAW or LPR/IPP) sends data to the device, often via a **print server** that shares queues.

steps.title: Print server benefits
steps.body: Central drivers, queue permissions, deployment by Group Policy (Deployed Printers / Point and Print), and one place to fix an IP change.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Installing random vendor drivers per PC; restarting the spooler on a print server in business hours without warning — it drops every queue.

cards.back: Common RAW TCP port for network printers
Lets clients download the driver from the print server
Newer driver model that clients can get without vendor-specific packages

lessons.title: Lab: Addressing and subnet maths

scenes.text: Two PCs are on the same switch but can't reach each other. One has mask 255.255.255.192.

steps.title: The basics
steps.body: An IPv4 address has 32 bits. The prefix (/24, /26) says how many are network bits. Usable hosts = 2^(32−prefix) − 2 (network and broadcast addresses).

steps.title: Worked example: /26
steps.body: /26 → 32−26 = 6 host bits → 2^6 = 64 addresses → 62 usable. Blocks start at .0, .64, .128, .192. So 10.20.14.57 is in .0–.63, but .200 is in .192–.255: different subnets → traffic must go via the gateway.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the −2; treating 169.254 as 'a valid IP'; mixing up /26 (255.255.255.192) and /28 (255.255.255.240).

lessons.title: TPM, protectors and recovery keys

story.title: Why the laptop asked for 48 digits

scenes.text: After a BIOS update Leela's laptop shows a blue BitLocker recovery screen asking for a 48-digit key.
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: How it works
steps.body: BitLocker encrypts the volume with a key that is sealed by the **TPM**, which only releases it if the boot measurements (firmware, boot manager, settings) match. Change those (BIOS update, boot order, Secure Boot off) and the TPM refuses → recovery.

steps.title: Protectors
steps.body: TPM, TPM+PIN, recovery password (48 digits in 8 groups of 6), recovery key file, password (data drives). The recovery password should be escrowed to AD DS or Entra ID before the user receives the device.

steps.title: Suspend before firmware work
steps.body: `Suspend-BitLocker -MountPoint C: -RebootCount 1` (or `manage-bde -protectors -disable C: -RebootCount 1`) lets one reboot pass without recovery, then protection resumes automatically.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Decrypting the drive to 'fix' recovery prompts; reading the key to someone who has not been identity-verified.

statements.s: A BIOS update without suspending BitLocker can trigger recovery mode.
The BitLocker recovery password has 32 digits.
statements.why: It has 48 digits in 8 groups of 6.
Suspension leaves data encrypted; the key is temporarily stored in the clear on disk until resume.

statements.s: Recovery keys should be escrowed to AD DS or Entra ID.
statements.why: Otherwise nobody can unlock the drive later.

quiz.q: What makes the TPM release the BitLocker key?
options: Boot measurements match what it sealed against

options: AD DS or Entra ID (or MBAM/Intune)

steps.title: Hyper-V
steps.body: A type-1 hypervisor: the Windows install you see becomes the **parent partition**; VMs are child partitions. Requires 64-bit CPU with virtualisation extensions and SLAT.

steps.title: Switches
steps.body: **External**: bound to a physical NIC — VMs reach the LAN. **Internal**: VMs + host only. **Private**: VMs only, isolated lab networks.

steps.title: Generation 2
steps.body: UEFI firmware, Secure Boot, boot from SCSI virtual disks, no emulated legacy devices, virtual TPM possible. Use Gen 2 for all modern Windows/Linux guests. Generation can't be changed after creation.

scenes.text: Someone took a checkpoint of SQL05 'before patching' — eight months ago. The host's D: is nearly full.

steps.title: How they work
steps.body: A checkpoint freezes the VHDX and writes changes to an **.avhdx** differencing disk. Every change grows the chain; performance and space suffer the longer it lives. **Production checkpoints** (default since 2016) use VSS in the guest for app consistency; **standard** checkpoints capture memory state too.

steps.body: `Checkpoint-VM -Name SQL05 -SnapshotName 'pre-CU-Nov'` · `Get-VMSnapshot -VMName SQL05` · `Remove-VMSnapshot -VMName SQL05 -Name 'pre-CU-Nov'` (merges into the parent; watch `Get-VM SQL05 | Select Status`) · `Restore-VMSnapshot` to roll back.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating checkpoints as backups; deleting .avhdx files by hand in Explorer (corrupts the chain); restoring a checkpoint of a domain controller without understanding USN rollback protections.

lessons.title: Lab: Hybrid identity concepts

scenes.text: Contoso uses AD on-prem and Microsoft 365 in the cloud. Users want one username and password.
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: Sync
steps.body: **Microsoft Entra Connect Sync** (installed on a member server) synchronises users, groups and devices from AD to Entra ID. Default scheduler: a delta sync every **30 minutes**. AD remains the source of authority for synced objects — edit them on-prem.

steps.title: Authentication options
steps.body:
- **Password hash synchronisation (PHS)**: a hash of the AD password hash is synced; cloud authenticates. Simplest, resilient, enables leaked-credential detection.
- **Pass-through authentication (PTA)**: cloud forwards password validation to on-prem agents.
- **Federation (AD FS)**: on-prem federation servers authenticate; most complex.
Seamless SSO can be added to PHS/PTA for domain-joined devices.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Editing a synced user's attributes in the cloud portal (overwritten or blocked); a .local UPN suffix that can't be verified in Entra — users end up with @tenant.onmicrosoft.com sign-in names.

scenes.text: 'The server feels slow' is not a diagnosis. Counters are.
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: Counters
steps.body:
- `\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time` — sustained > 85–90% is a CPU bottleneck

lessons.title: Lab: Types of change

scenes.text: Resetting a password, adding a DNS record, patching DCs, rebuilding a cluster — which need approval?
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Standard change**: pre-approved, low-risk, repeatable with a documented procedure (e.g. create a user, add a DNS A record via the approved template).
- **Normal change**: assessed and authorised (by change authority / CAB depending on risk).
- **Emergency change**: must be done urgently to fix or prevent a major incident; expedited authorisation, documented afterwards fully.

steps.title: Change vs request
steps.body: A password reset is a service request, not a change to a configuration item. Anything altering production configuration (GPO, firewall rule, DNS zone, server patch) is a change.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling everything 'emergency' to skip CAB; 'small' unregistered changes — the cause of many incidents.
